title: Subtree vs Submodule
description: Compare subtrees and submodules and choose the right approach for your project.

data.text: Subtrees and submodules both solve the problem of including external repositories, but they do so in fundamentally different ways. Choosing the wrong approach creates unnecessary complexity for your team. Understanding the trade-offs helps you make the right decision.

rows: External code lives in your repo

items: **Shared libraries**: Teams maintain the external repo independently
**Large dependencies**: You do not want to bloat your repository
**Separate release cycles**: The external repo has its own versioning
**Multiple consumers**: Many projects depend on the same external repo

data.title: Submodule use case: shared UI component library
data.code:
# Project A uses the shared UI library
git submodule add https://github.com/company/ui-lib.git packages/ui-lib

# Project B uses the same library
git submodule add https://github.com/company/ui-lib.git src/ui-lib

# Both projects track the same external repository
# and can update independently

items: **Vendored code**: You customize the external code and do not plan to push changes upstream
**Simple team workflows**: Developers should not need to learn submodule commands
**Small external repos**: The size impact is acceptable
**CI/CD simplicity**: Builds work without extra initialization steps

data.title: Subtree use case: vendored library
data.code:
# Embed a library you plan to customize
git subtree add --prefix=vendor/json-parser \
  https://github.com/example/json-parser.git \
  main --squash

# The library is now in vendor/json-parser/
# You can edit it freely without pushing upstream

# When upstream has fixes you want:
git subtree pull --prefix=vendor/json-parser \
  https://github.com/example/json-parser.git \
  main --squash

data.title: Avoid mixing subtrees and submodules
data.text: Using both subtrees and submodules in the same project creates confusion. Pick one approach and apply it consistently across the repository.

For many use cases, a package manager (npm, NuGet, pip, etc.) is a better choice than subtrees or submodules. Package managers handle versioning, updates, and dependency resolution without modifying your Git history.

data.title: Prefer package managers for standard dependencies
data.code:
# Instead of a submodule for a standard library:
npm install lodash

# Instead of a subtree for a .NET library:
dotnet add package Newtonsoft.Json

# Use subtrees/submodules only when:
# - No package manager exists for the dependency
# - You need to customize the dependency code
# - You need to track a specific commit for reproducibility

items.question: Can I convert a submodule to a subtree?
items.answer: Yes. Remove the submodule with git submodule deinit and git rm, then add the external repository as a subtree with git subtree add.

items.question: Can I convert a subtree to a submodule?
items.answer: Yes, but it requires extracting the subtree history and setting up a new submodule. It is easier to remove the subtree and add a new submodule.

items.question: Do subtrees work with GitHub Codespaces?
items.answer: Yes. Subtrees are just files in your repository, so Codespaces handles them like any other code.

items.question: Which approach does Git itself use?
items.answer: Git's own source code uses subtrees for some dependencies (e.g., the curl library). This demonstrates that subtrees are suitable even for large, mature projects.

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: Subtrees embed external code; submodules track external commits
Choose submodules for shared libraries with separate release cycles
Choose subtrees for vendored code and simple team workflows
Prefer package managers (npm, NuGet, pip) for standard dependencies
Avoid mixing subtrees and submodules in the same project
